newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices gain almost $1, led by U.S. gasoline.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices gain almost $1, led by U.S. gasoline.

text.p: World oil prices rose in late trade on Monday led by gains on New York gasoline futures, brokers said.

Brent crude oil gained almost $1 in a products-led rally which some attributed to the closure of Mexico's three crude ports because of bad weather. Other brokers said the gains were on good fundamental gasoline and heating oil demand in the United States.

The Mexican ports were closed on Monday as a cold front blew winds of up to 50 km (30 miles) an hour along the Gulf of Mexico. This cut Mexican crude oil exports by almost 1.5 million barrels per day.
World benchmark Brent Blend for January delivery was trading up 85 cents at $23.63 a barrel at 2040 GMT.
Prices had been pulled down earlier in the day after Iraq said it had signed oil export agreements with foreign oil companies under a delayed "oil-for-food" agreement with the United Nations.
Iraq said the state-owned oil company SOMO had signed contracts with foreign companies to sell oil under the U.N. plan allowing Baghdad to sell crude oil to buy food and medicines.

"The Oil Ministry has begun signing contracts with international oil firms within the framework of the memorandum of understanding (with the United Nations)," Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf said in remarks published in Baghdad's state-run newspapers.

Iraqi oil exports have been banned under a U.N. embargo imposed after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990. Under the U.N. agreement, Iraq will be allowed exports totalling $2.0 billion in value for six months.

The statement did not say which oil companies were involved in negotiating term contracts with Iraq, which produced 3.5 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil before 1990 and was the largest Gulf oil producer after Saudi Arabia.

The incremental Iraqi barrels were factored into the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) ceiling, which was set at 25.03 million bpd last June and frozen until mid-1997 at last week's OPEC meeting in Vienna.
Oil analysts say the market appeared comfortable with the potential addition to winter supplies and prices have held up.

"It is very difficult to judge what the market will do but it's fairly stable at present, which suggests that fundamentals are quite supportive," said Russ Hill, senior trader at the London office of Austrian oil company OMV.
